raw_text:
HIP OSTEOARTHRITIS (Hip OA)

Age

>45 years (Strong indicator)

<45 years



Where is the pain located?

Groin/anterior hip (Classic)

Lateral hip

Buttock



Recent history of fall or trauma to the hip?

Yes (Rule out fracture)

No



How did the pain begin?

Gradual, insidious

Sudden



How will you describe the pain?

Dull, aching

Sharp



What aggravates the pain?

Walking, weight-bearing, stairs

Rest



Is the pain relieved by rest?

Yes (Mechanical pattern)

No (Consider red flag)



Morning stiffness

<60 minutes (Typical OA)

>60 minutes (Consider inflammatory condition)



Difficulty with daily activities (e.g., shoes/socks)?

Yes (Hip mobility restriction)

No



Reduced walking tolerance?

Yes

No



Crepitus or grinding sensation in the hip?

Yes

No



Is sleep affected by pain?

Yes (Advanced OA or red flag)

No



Does pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Rule out lumbar spine pathology)

No (Rule out labral tear)



Previous history of hip injury or surgery?



Yes (May predispose to OA)

No



Do you feel stiffness after periods of inactivity (e.g., sitting)?

Yes (Typical OA feature)

No



Do symptoms worsen with prolonged standing or walking?

Yes (Load-related pain)

No



Do symptoms improve with reduced activity?

Yes (Mechanical OA pattern)

No



Do you experience clicking, locking, or catching?

Yes (Rule out labral pathology)

No



Do you feel instability or giving way?

Yes (Consider muscle weakness or other pathology)

No



Objective / Observation

Reduced hip internal rotation?

Yes (Key OA finding)

No



Pain at end-range hip flexion/internal rotation?

Yes

No



Is antalgic gait present?

Yes

No



Trendelenburg gait/sign?

Yes (Gluteal weakness)

No



Muscle weakness (gluteals)?

Yes

No



Red Flag

Hip OA itself is non-emergency, but must rule out serious pathology.

Inability to bear weight?

Yes (Serious pathology)

No



Severe Do you experience night pain not relieved by rest?

Yes (Possible malignancy/infection)

No



Unexplained weight loss?

Yes (Possible malignancy)

No

Fever or systemic illness?

Yes (Possible infection)

No



Pain rapidly worsening without clear cause?

Yes (Red flag)

No



History of cancer?

Yes (Metastasis risk)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

FABER Test (Patrick’s Test)

Patient is supine. The affected leg is placed in flexion, abduction, and external rotation (figure-4 position). Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the knee.

Sign is positive if pain is reproduced in the groin or there is restricted movement.

If positive, indicates hip joint pathology such as OA.



FADIR Test

Patient is supine. Examiner flexes the hip to 90°, then adducts and internally rotates the hip.

Sign is positive if groin pain is reproduced.

If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology (OA or FAI).



Scour Test

Patient is supine. Examiner flexes and adducts the hip, then applies axial compression while moving the hip in an arc.

Sign is positive if pain, grinding, or crepitus is felt.

If positive, suggests hip joint degeneration (OA).



Log Roll Test

Patient is supine with legs extended. Examiner gently rolls the leg internally and externally.

Sign is positive if pain or increased external rotation is noted.

If positive, indicates intra-articular hip pathology.



Trendelenburg Test

Patient stands on one leg. Examiner observes pelvic alignment.

Sign is positive if pelvis drops on the opposite side.

If positive, indicates gluteus medius weakness associated with hip OA.





GREATER TROCHANTERIC PAIN SYNDROME (GTPS)

Age

30–60 years (Common demographic for GTPS)

<30 years (Consider muscle injury or FAI)



Where is the pain located?

Lateral hip (Classic GTPS)

Groin (Suggests OA or FAI)

Buttock (Suggests lumbar/deep gluteal)



Recent history of fall or trauma?

Yes (Rule out fracture/contusion)

No (Supports GTPS)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual (Typical GTPS – tendinopathy)

Sudden (Consider muscle tear)



How will you describe the pain?

Aching, localized (GTPS pattern)

Sharp (Consider tear or acute injury)



What aggravates the pain?

Lying on affected side (Highly specific for GTPS)

Walking, prolonged standing (Load compression → GTPS)

Deep flexion/squatting (Suggests FAI)



Is the Is the pain relieved by rest?

Yes (Mechanical condition → GTPS)

No (Consider alternative pathology)



Do you experience pain when climbing stairs?

Yes (Gluteal tendon loading → GTPS)

No



Does the pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Suggests lumbar origin)

No (Supports GTPS)



Is sleep affected (due to lying on side)?

Yes (Strong GTPS indicator)

No

Tenderness when pressing the side of the hip?

Yes (Key hallmark of GTPS)

No (Less likely GTPS)



Any previous hip or lower limb injury?

Yes (Predisposing factor)

No



Objective / Observation

Tenderness over greater trochanter?

Yes (Primary diagnostic sign of GTPS)

No



Pain with resisted hip abduction?

Yes (Gluteal tendinopathy → GTPS)

No



Single-leg stance (30 sec) reproduces pain?

Yes (Highly sensitive for GTPS)

No



Trendelenburg sign?

Yes (Gluteal weakness in GTPS)

No



Red Flag

Any history of trauma?

Yes (Rule out fracture)

No



Do you experience Do you experience night pain not relieved by rest?

Yes (Possible malignancy)

No



Do you have fever or systemic illness?

Yes (Possible infection)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Single-Leg Stance Test

Patient stands on the affected leg for up to 30 seconds.

Sign is positive if lateral hip pain is reproduced within 30 seconds.

If positive, indicates gluteal tendinopathy associated with GTPS.



Resisted External Derotation Test

Patient lies supine with hip flexed to 90°. Examiner passively externally rotates the hip, then asks patient to return leg to neutral against resistance.

Sign is positive if pain is reproduced over the lateral hip.

If positive, suggests gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy (GTPS).



Ober’s Test

Patient lies on side with unaffected leg down. Examiner extends and abducts the affected hip, then allows it to drop into adduction.

Sign is positive if the leg remains abducted and does not drop.

If positive, indicates ITB tightness contributing to GTPS.



Trendelenburg Test

Patient stands on one leg while examiner observes pelvic alignment.

Sign is positive if pelvis drops on the contralateral side.

If positive, indicates gluteal weakness associated with GTPS.





FEMOROACETABULAR IMPINGEMENT (FAI)

Age

15–40 years (Strong FAI group)

>40 years (Consider OA)



Where is the pain located?

Groin (Classic FAI)

Lateral hip (GTPS)

Buttock (Lumbar/deep gluteal)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual with activity (FAI pattern)

Sudden (Labral tear or injury)



How will you describe the pain?

Sharp/deep (FAI intra-articular)

Dull (OA)



What aggravates the pain?

Sitting for long periods (Hip flexion → FAI)

Squatting/deep flexion (Classic FAI)

Walking (OA more likely)



Is the pain relieved by rest?

Yes (Mechanical → FAI)

No (Consider other pathology)



Do you feel clicking or catching?

Yes (Suggests labral involvement with FAI)

No



Do you feel stiffness in the hip?

Yes (FAI/OA)

No



Does pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Suggests lumbar origin)

No



Are you involved in sports or repetitive hip movements?

Yes (FAI risk factor)

No



Objective / Observation

Is internal rotation reduced in flexion?

Yes (Key FAI sign)

No



Is there pain with flexion + adduction + internal rotation?

Yes (Classic FAI)

No



Is hip ROM asymmetry?

Yes (Supports FAI)

No



Red Flag

Is the pain severe and constant?

Yes (Not typical FAI → investigate)

No



Do you experience night pain not relieved by rest?

Yes (Serious pathology)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

FADIR Test (Flexion, Adduction, Internal Rotation)

Patient is supine. Examiner flexes the hip to 90°, then adducts and internally rotates the hip.

Sign is positive if groin pain is reproduced.

If positive, indicates femoroacetabular impingement or intra-articular pathology.



FABER Test (Patrick’s Test)

Patient is supine. The leg is placed in flexion, abduction, and external rotation (figure-4 position). Examiner applies downward pressure on the knee.

Sign is positive if pain is reproduced or there is asymmetry compared to the other side.

If positive, suggests hip joint pathology such as FAI.



Scour Test



Patient is supine. Examiner flexes and adducts the hip, then applies axial compression while moving the hip through an arc.

Sign is positive if pain, clicking, or grinding is reproduced.

If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology such as FAI or labral involvement.



Internal Rotation Overpressure Test

Patient is supine with hip flexed to 90°. Examiner applies internal rotation with overpressure.

Sign is positive if groin pain or restriction is noted.

If positive, suggests FAI due to limited internal rotation.





HIP LABRAL TEAR

Age

20–50 years (Common labral group)

<20 or >50 (Consider other pathology)



Where is the pain located?

Deep groin (Classic labral tear)

Lateral hip (GTPS)

Buttock (Lumbar)



How did the pain begin?

Sudden or with twisting injury (Labral tear)

Gradual (FAI/OA)



How will you describe the pain?

Sharp, catching (Labral tear)

Dull (OA)



Do you experience clicking, locking, or catching?

Yes (Strong labral tear indicator)

No



What aggravates the pain?

Pivoting/twisting (Labral tear)

Walking (OA)



Do you feel instability in the hip?

Yes (Labral involvement)

No



Is the pain relieved by rest?

Yes (Mechanical)

No



Does pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Lumbar origin)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there pain with combined flexion + rotation?

Yes (Labral tear)

No



Is clicking reproduced during movement?

Yes (Strong labral sign)

No



Red Flag

Trauma with inability to bear weight?

Yes (Fracture)

No



Do you experience night pain/systemic symptoms?

Yes (Serious pathology)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

FADIR Test

Patient is supine. Examiner flexes, adducts, and internally rotates the hip.

Sign is positive if groin pain or clicking is reproduced.

If positive, indicates labral pathology or FAI.



Scour Test

Patient is supine. Examiner applies axial load while moving the hip in a circular motion.

Sign is positive if pain, clicking, or catching is felt.

If positive, suggests labral tear or intra-articular pathology.



Log Roll Test

Patient is supine with legs extended. Examiner gently rolls the leg internally and externally.

Sign is positive if increased external rotation or pain is observed.

If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology such as a labral tear.



Thomas Test (Modified)

Patient lies supine and pulls one knee to chest while the other leg hangs off the table.

Sign is positive if the hanging leg produces hip pain or clicking.

If positive, may indicate labral irritation or associated hip pathology.





AVASCULAR NECROSIS (AVN)

Age

20–50 years (Common AVN group; younger than OA → key differentiator)

>50 years (Consider OA)



Where is the pain located?

Deep groin (Classic AVN location)

Buttock (Less specific; consider SIJ/lumbar)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual, progressive (Typical AVN pattern)

Sudden (Consider fracture)



How will you describe the pain?

Deep, aching (AVN)

Sharp (Consider labral tear or acute injury)



What aggravates the pain?

Weight-bearing (Common but not specific)

Rest (If worse at rest → red flag)



Is the pain relieved by rest?

No (CRITICAL → suggests AVN over OA)

Yes (More consistent with OA)



Do you experience pain at rest?

Yes (Strong AVN indicator → red flag)

No



Do you have night pain?

Yes (Red flag → AVN/malignancy/infection)

No



Risk factors (steroids, alcohol, sickle cell)?

Yes (VERY STRONG AVN indicator)

No



How will you describe the progression of the symptoms?

Rapid worsening over weeks–months (Suggests AVN)

Slow progression over years (Suggests OA)



Is your walking tolerance reduced?

Yes (Progressive joint collapse → AVN)

No



Does pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Suggests lumbar origin, not AVN)

No (Supports hip origin)



Objective / Observation

Is there pain with multiple hip movements (not just end-range)?

Yes (Diffuse joint involvement → AVN)

No



Is internal rotation reduced?

Yes (Seen in AVN but less specific than OA)

No



Antalgic gait?

Yes (Pain avoidance → AVN progression)

No



Red Flag

Do you experience night pain not relieved by rest?

Yes (Serious pathology → AVN/malignancy)

No



Do you experience pain at rest?

Yes (Strong AVN red flag)

No



Rapid unexplained worsening?

Yes (AVN suspicion)

No



Any history of steroid use/alcohol/sickle cell?

Yes (Major AVN risk factor)

No







SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Log Roll Test

Patient is supine with legs extended. Examiner gently rolls the leg internally and externally.

Sign is positive if pain is reproduced in neutral rotation.

If positive, indicates early intra-articular pathology (AVN suspicion).



FADIR Test

Patient is supine. Examiner flexes, adducts, and internally rotates the hip.

Sign is positive if groin pain is reproduced.

If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology (use red flags to suspect AVN).



FABER Test

Patient is supine. The leg is placed in flexion, abduction, and external rotation. Examiner applies downward pressure.

Sign is positive if groin pain is reproduced.

If positive, indicates hip joint pathology.





SNAPPING HIP SYNDROME

Age

15–40 years (Common in active individuals)

>40 years (Consider OA or other pathology)



Primary symptom (snapping sensation)

Yes (DEFINING FEATURE → required for diagnosis)

No (Not snapping hip)



Where is the snapping located?

Anterior hip (Iliopsoas → internal snapping)

Lateral hip (ITB → external snapping)

Deep groin with clicking (Consider labral tear instead)



How did the symptoms begin?

Gradual with activity (Typical snapping hip)

Sudden (Less common; consider injury)



How will you describe the pain?

Painless snapping (Benign form)

Painful snapping (Pathological → requires attention)



What aggravates the pain?

Repetitive hip flexion/extension (Running, dancing) (Classic trigger)

Deep flexion/pivoting (Suggests FAI/labral tear)



Do you experience clicking, locking, or catching?

Yes (Suggests labral tear, not isolated snapping hip)

No (Supports snapping hip)



Is the pain relieved by rest?

Yes (Mechanical pattern → snapping hip)

No (Consider alternative pathology)



Does pain radiate below the knee?

Yes (Suggests lumbar origin)

No (Supports hip origin)



Objective / Observation



Is there visible or palpable snapping during movement?

Yes (PRIMARY diagnostic sign)

No



Is snapping reproduced with hip flexion-extension?

Yes (Confirms snapping hip)

No



Tenderness over iliopsoas or ITB?

Yes (Supports subtype identification)

No



Red Flag

Do you experience severe and persistent pain unrelated to movement?

Yes (Not typical snapping hip → investigate)

No



Do you experience night pain/systemic symptoms?

Yes (Serious pathology)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Dynamic Hip Movement Test

Patient actively flexes and extends the hip while examiner palpates.

Sign is positive if snapping is reproduced.

If positive, confirms snapping hip syndrome.



Ober’s Test (External Snapping)

Patient lies on side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then allows it to drop.

Sign is positive if the leg remains abducted.

If positive, indicates ITB tightness contributing to lateral snapping.



Thomas Test (Internal Snapping)

Patient lies supine and pulls one knee to chest while the other leg hangs.

Sign is positive if snapping or pain occurs in anterior hip.

If positive, suggests iliopsoas involvement.
